entry: Paraguayan army general and military dictator, president of Paraguay (1954–1989). After fighting in the Chaco War against [[Bolivia]], he seized power in a coup in May 1954 and was elected unopposed that year. He was reelected seven times, maintaining power by electoral fraud from 1958 to 1988. He suspended civil liberties under a state of siege that allowed indefinite detention without trial, and political opponents faced violent repression, including torture. His government built the [[Itaipu Dam]] with Brazil. He was overthrown in a 1989 coup led by his confidant Andrés Rodríguez and went into exile in Brazil. Among 20th-century Latin American leaders, only [[Fidel Castro]] served longer. His Colorado Party has retained power since, ruling through clientelistic practices.

Branch of mathematics concerned with the zeros of polynomial equations, using mainly [[Commutative algebra|commutative algebra]] to solve geometric problems. Its basic objects, algebraic varieties, are the solution sets of systems of polynomial equations; examples include lines, circles, ellipses and elliptic curves. The field has close links with [[Complex analysis|complex analysis]], [[Topology|topology]] and [[Number theory|number theory]]. In the 20th century it split into subareas, including real algebraic geometry and arithmetic geometry, which studies varieties over fields used in number theory. Grothendieck's scheme theory allowed [[Sheaf (mathematics)|sheaf theory]] to be applied to varieties, and Wiles's proof of [[Fermat's Last Theorem]] is cited as an example of the power of this approach.

Finite-degree extension of the [[Rational number|rational numbers]]. A [[Field (mathematics)|field]] K containing ℚ, and of finite dimension as a vector space over ℚ, is called a number field; that dimension is its degree. The study of such fields is the central topic of [[Algebraic number theory]], which uses algebraic methods to reveal hidden structures behind the rational numbers. The rationals themselves are the smallest and most basic example. The Gaussian rationals, ℚ(i), with elements a + bi for rational a and b, are the first historically nontrivial example and have dimension two over ℚ. For any square-free integer d, the quadratic field ℚ(√d) is obtained by adjoining the square root of d. The cyclotomic field ℚ(ζₙ), formed by adjoining a primitive n-th root of unity, has dimension φ(n) over ℚ, where φ is the Euler totient function. Unlike the integers, the ring of algebraic integers in a number field need not be a unique factorization domain.

Branch of [[Number theory|number theory]] that applies the techniques of [[Abstract algebra|abstract algebra]] to the integers, the rational numbers and their generalizations. Questions are expressed through algebraic objects such as algebraic number fields, their rings of integers, finite fields and function fields. Properties such as unique factorization and the behavior of ideals can resolve questions such as the existence of solutions to [[Diophantine equation|Diophantine equations]]. Its origins lie in the work of the 3rd-century Alexandrian mathematician [[Diophantus]]. [[Pierre de Fermat]] conjectured [[Fermat's Last Theorem]] in 1637, and no successful proof was published until 1995; the unsolved problem stimulated the field's development in the 19th century. [[Carl Friedrich Gauss|Gauss]]'s *Disquisitiones Arithmeticae*, written in 1798 and published in 1801, brought earlier results into a systematic framework. In papers of 1838 and 1839, [[Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet|Dirichlet]] proved the first class number formula for quadratic forms.

Nonempty set with operations obeying specified axioms. An algebraic structure consists of an underlying set, called the carrier set, a collection of operations on it, typically binary operations such as addition and multiplication, and a finite set of identities, called axioms, that these operations must satisfy. Structures can be built on others: a [[Vector space|vector space]] involves a [[Field (mathematics)|field]] of scalars and an operation of scalar multiplication. Common axioms include commutativity, x∗y = y∗x, and associativity, (x∗y)∗z = x∗(y∗z). The study of algebraic structures is commonly called [[Abstract algebra|abstract algebra]]. Universal algebra formalizes the general theory, and [[Category theory|category theory]] studies structures together with the homomorphisms between them.

Branch of mathematics using tools from [[Abstract algebra|abstract algebra]] to study topological spaces. Its basic goal is to find algebraic invariants that classify [[Topological space|topological spaces]] up to homeomorphism, though usually most classify them up to [[Homotopy|homotopy]] equivalence. Homotopy groups record the basic shape, or holes, of a space; the first, the [[Fundamental group]], records information about loops. [[Homology (mathematics)|Homology]] associates a sequence of abelian groups to a space, and cohomology, its algebraic dual, assigns invariants with a more refined structure. Results often concern global aspects of manifolds, such as Poincaré duality. In knot theory, a knot is an embedding of a [[Circle]] in three-dimensional [[Euclidean space]], and two knots are equivalent if one can be deformed into the other without cutting. Algebraic topology also gives a convenient proof that any subgroup of a free group is free.

Solution set of a system of polynomial equations, the central object of [[Algebraic geometry|algebraic geometry]]. Classically, it is defined over the real or [[Complex number|complex numbers]]. Definitions differ: some require irreducibility, meaning the set is not the union of two smaller closed sets in the Zariski topology, and call non-irreducible sets algebraic sets. Varieties of dimension one are algebraic curves, and those of dimension two are algebraic surfaces. The [[Fundamental theorem of algebra|fundamental theorem of algebra]] links algebra and geometry, since a monic polynomial in one variable is determined by its roots in the complex plane. Hilbert's Nullstellensatz generalizes this, establishing a correspondence between ideals of polynomial rings and algebraic sets. In modern scheme theory, an algebraic variety over a field is an integral scheme of finite type over that field.

1954–1962 war of Algerian independence from [[France]]. Fought between France and the Algerian National Liberation Front (FLN), it was a guerrilla war marked by war crimes that also became a civil war between communities. It began on November 1, 1954, with coordinated FLN attacks. The brutality of French methods alienated support in France, and after mass demonstrations and a [[United Nations]] resolution recognizing the right to independence, [[Charles de Gaulle]] opened negotiations with the FLN. The Évian Accords, signed in March 1962, were approved by referendums in France and Algeria. The war caused between 400,000 and 1.5 million deaths among Algerians, 25,600 French soldiers and 6,000 Europeans. War crimes included massacres, rape and [[Torture|torture]], and the French relocated over 2 million Algerians to camps. About 900,000 European Algerians (pieds-noirs) fled to France after independence, and many Harkis, Algerians who had served with the French army, were murdered.

Indigenous language family of [[North America|North America]]. Most Algic languages belong to the Algonquian subfamily, spoken across a broad area from the [[Rocky Mountains|Rocky Mountains]] to Atlantic Canada. Yurok and Wiyot, spoken in northwestern [[California|California]], are not closely related to each other. All Algic languages descend from Proto-Algic, a second-order proto-language estimated to have been spoken about 5,000 years ago and reconstructed from Proto-Algonquian and the Wiyot and Yurok languages. Edward Sapir first proposed in 1913 that Wiyot and Yurok were related to Algonquian, and he applied the term Algic to the larger family. Michelson argued against the relationship, which is now widely accepted, but most specialists reject the "Ritwan" grouping of Wiyot and Yurok.

Capital and largest city of [[Algeria]], on the Mediterranean coast (urban area pop., 2025: 4,325,000). Algiers lies on the Bay of Algiers, surrounded by the Mitidja Plain and mountain ranges. It was formally founded in 972 by Buluggin ibn Ziri, and its history goes back to a Phoenician trading settlement; it came under Numidian, [[Roman Empire|Roman]] and Islamic rule. It became the capital of the Ottoman Regency of Algiers in 1516, a status it held until the French invasion of 1830, after which it was the capital of French Algeria. It was briefly the administrative center of Free France from 1942 to 1944 and has been the capital of independent Algeria since 1962. The historic Casbah, a [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]], blends Algerian, Ottoman and Andalusian architecture. Algiers hosted the 1975 Mediterranean Games and is the seat of the Consultative Council of the Arab [[Maghreb|Maghreb]] Union.

Palace and fortress complex in [[Granada]], Spain. Begun in 1238 by Muhammad I ibn al-Ahmar, first Nasrid sultan and founder of the Emirate of Granada, the last Muslim state of [[Al-Andalus|al-Andalus]], it is the only well-preserved palace from the medieval Islamic world. The complex was a self-contained city on the Sabika hill, with a Friday mosque, baths, workshops and houses. Its palaces are known for courtyards with water features, tile mosaics, carved stucco and muqarnas vaulting. After the [[Reconquista]] ended in 1492, Ferdinand and Isabella used the site as their royal court, and in 1526 Charles V commissioned a Renaissance palace beside the Nasrid palaces. Troops of [[Napoleon]] destroyed parts of the complex in 1812. Washington Irving's *Tales of the Alhambra* (1832) brought it international attention, and it is now one of Spain's major tourist attractions and a [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

Yemeni military officer and politician, president of North Yemen (1978–1990) and of unified Yemen (1990–2012). A veteran of the North Yemen civil war, he took power after the assassination of Ahmad al-Ghashmi in 1978 and presided over the 1990 unification with South Yemen. After southern forces were defeated in the 1994 civil war, he ruled by decree and was confirmed in elections in 1999 and 2006. His opposition to the [[Gulf War|Gulf War]] alienated the United States and [[Saudi Arabia]], but after he consolidated power he drew closer to Western powers in the war on terror. Protests during the [[Arab Spring]] forced his resignation in 2012, and Abdrabbuh Mansur Hadi succeeded him. In May 2015 Saleh openly allied with the Houthis, who had captured [[Sanaa]] during the [[Yemeni civil war (2014–present)|Yemeni civil war]]. He later broke with them and was killed by a Houthi sniper. Accounts differed on whether he was killed in his car or at his house.

Indian Hindustani classical musician and virtuoso sarod player of the Maihar gharana. Trained from childhood by his father, Ustad Allauddin Khan, he became one of the most celebrated Indian classical musicians of the 20th century, known for technical virtuosity and emotional intensity. He composed several ragas, including Chandranandan, and wrote film scores, among them for [[Satyajit Ray|Satyajit Ray]]'s *Devi* (1960). On his first visit to the United States, in 1955, he recorded *Music of India: Morning and Evening Ragas* in a [[Museum of Modern Art|Museum of Modern Art]] guest house in New York; it is generally described as the first album of Indian classical music issued in the West. He founded the Ali Akbar College of Music in [[Kolkata|Calcutta]] in 1956, followed by colleges in California and in [[Basel|Basel]], Switzerland. He received India's second-highest civilian honour, the Padma Vibhushan, in 1989.

headword: Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves
sort_key: ali baba and the forty thieves
entry: Arabic folk tale added to *One Thousand and One Nights* in the 18th century by Antoine Galland. Galland heard it from the Syrian storyteller Hanna Diyab, who came from [[Aleppo]] in modern-day [[Syria]] and told it in [[Paris]]; Galland's French version is the earliest known text. In the tale, Ali Baba, a poor woodcutter, overhears forty thieves and discovers their treasure cave, which opens to the words "open sesame." He takes only a bag of gold, but his greedy brother Cassim learns the secret, enters the cave, forgets the words to leave, and is killed by the thieves. Morgiana, the clever slave-girl who foils the thieves, later marries Ali Baba's son. The story has been widely retold and performed, especially for children, with its violent elements often removed. An Arabic manuscript once claimed to be a source was later found to be a counterfeit.

Chinese multinational technology company specializing in e-commerce, retail, Internet and [[Cloud computing|cloud computing]] services. Jack Ma and 17 friends and students founded it in [[Hangzhou]] on June 28, 1999, initially as the B2B marketplace Alibaba.com. The name comes from the character Ali Baba in *One Thousand and One Nights*. In 2003 Ma created the consumer marketplace Taobao to compete with [[EBay|eBay]], which had announced its expansion into China; Taobao surpassed eBay in 2007. [[Yahoo|Yahoo]] bought a 40% stake in 2005 for US$1 billion. Alibaba's initial public offering on the [[New York Stock Exchange|New York Stock Exchange]] in September 2014 raised US$25 billion, then the largest IPO in history. Its marketplaces include Alibaba.com, Taobao and Tmall, the largest B2B, C2C and B2C platforms in the world.

Children's novel by [[Lewis Carroll|Lewis Carroll]], published in 1865. Its heroine, Alice, falls through a rabbit hole into a world of anthropomorphic creatures, an example of literary nonsense. The book's [[Fantasy|fantasy]] and its play with [[Logic|logic]] gave it lasting appeal to adults as well as children. John Tenniel provided 42 wood-engraved illustrations for the original edition. Carroll first told the story on July 4, 1862, during a boat trip with the daughters of his friend Henry Liddell, and later wrote out the manuscript, now held by the [[British Library|British Library]]. The novel is credited with helping end an era of didacticism in [[Children's literature|children's literature]]. It has never been out of print and has been translated into 174 languages. Its legacy includes adaptations for film, ballet, [[Opera|opera]] and [[Musical theatre|musical theatre]]. Carroll published the sequel *Through the Looking-Glass* in 1871.

Group of highly reactive metallic elements in Group 1 of the [[Periodic table|periodic table]]. The alkali metals are [[Lithium|lithium]], sodium, potassium, rubidium, cesium and [[Francium|francium]]. They are soft, shiny metals that readily lose their outermost electron to form +1 ions, and their similar properties show clear group trends. They tarnish rapidly in air and must be stored under oil; cesium is the most reactive metal. All of them react with water, the heavier ones more vigorously. Sodium is the most abundant in nature, while francium is so radioactive that only minute traces occur. Rubidium and cesium are used in [[Atomic clock|atomic clocks]], and cesium clocks form the basis of the second. [[Sodium chloride|Table salt]] has been used since antiquity, and lithium is used in batteries. Sodium, potassium and possibly lithium are essential elements.

Iranian cleric and politician, supreme leader of Iran (1989–2026). A student of [[Ruhollah Khomeini|Ruhollah Khomeini]], he was president from 1981 to 1989, during the [[Iran–Iraq War|Iran–Iraq War]], and built close ties with the [[Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps|Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps]]. Elected supreme leader after Khomeini's death, he held the office for 36 years, the longest of any supreme leader. Critics describe his government as authoritarian, citing political repression and the persecution of dissidents. Substantial spending on the nuclear program contributed to international sanctions. He was assassinated during a war with Israel.

British actress of Indian descent, known mainly for Hindi films. She has received a National Film Award and seven Filmfare Awards, including the National Film Award for Best Actress for *Gangubai Kathiawadi* (2022). One of India's highest-paid actresses, she founded the production company Eternal Sunshine Productions in 2019 and the sustainable clothing brand Ed-a-Mamma. She is married to actor [[Ranbir Kapoor|Ranbir Kapoor]].

American singer and songwriter, called the "Godfather of Shock Rock." Born Vincent Damon Furnier in Detroit, he fronted the band Alice Cooper, which originated in [[Phoenix, Arizona|Phoenix]] in 1964. Its singles included "I'm Eighteen" and "School's Out." After the band broke up, Furnier legally adopted the band's name for a solo career that began with the concept album *Welcome to My Nightmare* (1975). His theatrical shows, with horror imagery and props, helped shape heavy metal. The original band was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame|Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2011.

American rock band formed in [[Seattle|Seattle]] in 1987. Rooted in heavy metal and associated with grunge, the band is known for harmonized vocals between Layne Staley and Jerry Cantrell. It rose to fame in the early 1990s alongside [[Nirvana (band)|Nirvana]] and [[Pearl Jam|Pearl Jam]]. Its albums *Jar of Flies* (1994) and *Alice in Chains* (1995) both topped the Billboard 200. After Staley's death the band went on hiatus, then reunited with William DuVall as a vocalist. It has sold over 30 million RIAA-certified records in the United States.

Town in the [[Northern Territory|Northern Territory]], Australia. Locally called The Alice, it is the third-largest settlement in the territory and is roughly equidistant from [[Adelaide|Adelaide]] and Darwin. It was named after Alice, Lady Todd, wife of the telegraph pioneer Charles Todd. The town straddles the usually dry Todd River, north of the MacDonnell Ranges, in the arid Red Centre. Its population was 34,783 as of June 2025. The Arrernte people have lived in the area for at least 30,000 years.

American singer, songwriter and pianist. Classically trained, she was signed by [[Columbia Records|Columbia Records]] at 15. Her debut album, *Songs in A Minor* (2001), sold over 12 million copies and won five Grammy Awards. Hits include "Fallin'" and "No One." She has sold over 90 million records worldwide and has received 17 Grammy Awards. Her Broadway musical *Hell's Kitchen* won two Tony Awards. She co-founded the HIV and AIDS charity Keep a Child Alive in 2003.

Swedish actress and former ballet dancer. She won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for playing Gerda Wegener in *The Danish Girl* (2015). She was also nominated for a BAFTA Award for playing a humanoid robot in *Ex Machina* (2014), and she starred in *Jason Bourne* (2016) and *Tomb Raider* (2018). Her early career was in Swedish film and television, and she won the Guldbagge Award for Best Actress for *Pure*. She married actor [[Michael Fassbender|Michael Fassbender]] in 2017.

1979 science fiction horror film directed by [[Ridley Scott|Ridley Scott]]. A commercial starship crew investigates a derelict ship and is hunted by a deadly [[Extraterrestrial life|extraterrestrial]] creature designed by the Swiss artist H. R. Giger. *Alien* won the Academy Award for Best Visual Effects and was later reassessed as one of the greatest science fiction and horror films. In 2002 the [[Library of Congress|Library of Congress]] selected it for the National Film Registry. Its success spawned a franchise, and the story of [[Sigourney Weaver|Sigourney Weaver]]'s character became the core of the sequels *Aliens* (1986), *Alien 3* (1992) and *Alien Resurrection* (1997).
